aberration: Sounds like “a bear ration”: a bear showing up in your ration line is a departure from the normal.
Ab (away) + errare (wander): one sheep that wanders off from the flock. A glitch in the data.
acrimony: Acre = sharp. Acrid smoke, acrimonious words: both sting the throat.
Picture a Paris dinner where the cheese talk turns bitter: every sentence is vinaigrette, no oil.
amalgam: Al-chemy gave us amal-gam: the mercury-and-silver mix in a dental filling. Any blend of unlike things.
Ama + gam: “a mass of gum” stuck together from different flavours.
ambiguous: Ambi (both) + agere (drive): a car steering both left and right at once.
Un panneau qui indique deux directions: you can’t tell which one is meant.
ambivalent: Ambi (both) + valent (strength): two equally strong feelings. Hold two bags of equal weight: you can’t move.
“Ambi-valent” = bi-valent: you love it and hate it, like quitting a job you also need.
amenable: “Amen-able”: someone who says Amen, easily agrees. A choir member who goes along with everything.
À mener: easy to lead, like a docile horse.
amorphous: A (without) + morph (shape): a blob. Think of a jellyfish on the sand.
Morphing in Photoshop stopped halfway: no defined outline, an amorphous cloud.
anomalous: An + homalos (even): a bump on a flat road. The anomaly is the odd one out.
A penguin in the Sahara: anomalous, it doesn’t belong to the pattern.
artful: Art-ful here = full of artifice: a magician’s sleight of hand, not a painter’s brush.
The Artful Dodger: a clever pickpocket in Oliver Twist. Smart and sly.
auspicious: Auspice: an omen. Sous de bons auspices = a good start, like a lucky sunrise on your first day.
Think “a spicy start”: a hot, promising beginning. Favourable signs.
belie: Be + lie: your face lies. A huge smile that belies the fear inside.
To make a lie of: his calm manner belies his panic, the surface is hiding the truth.
betray: Trahir: the body betrays you. A blush betrays the lie you told.
Be + tray: you leave the tray, and the secret drops. Unintentional reveal.
calumny: “Call-um-ny”: you call someone horrible names that aren’t true. A calomnie in the press.
Calomnie: the rumour that sticks. Calumny = a lie with a goal, to ruin a name.
castigate: Castigate = “cast a gate”: you slam the gate of criticism on someone.
Châtier: the strict headmaster who punishes with words as much as with the cane.
censure: Censor + sure: a committee sure that you were wrong. Formal blame.
Un blâme officiel: the letter in your file after a vote of censure.
chastise: Chaste + rise: you tell off a child to “rise to chaste behaviour”. Scold.
Sounds like “chase-tise”: chasing someone with a scolding.
commensurate: Com + mensura (measure): same measuring tape for both. Pay measured against effort.
Commensurate = “common measure”: size of the reward matches the size of the work.
demur: Demurrer in French: to hesitate, linger. “De-murmur”: you murmur an objection instead of agreeing.
The pause before “yes”: you demur because you aren’t convinced.
disinterested: Dis-interested = no stake: a referee who doesn’t care who wins. Opposite of biased.
Remember: dis-interest = impartial; un-interested = bored. A judge should be the first.
egregious: E + grex (flock): sticks out of the flock like a black sheep. A glaring error.
“Egg-regious”: a rotten egg in a basket of fresh ones, impossible not to notice.
enervate: E + nerve: you take the nerve out. A heat wave enervates you; you flop on the sofa.
False friend: énerver = annoy; enervate = drain. Think “energy gone”.
equivocal: Equi + vocal: two voices of equal volume, saying different things.
Un oui qui veut dire non: an equivocal answer, impossible to pin down.
extant: Ex + stare: still standing. Like the Parthenon, one of the few extant Greek temples.
The opposite of extinct. Extant = it didn’t die out.
frugal: Fruit: frugal = eats what the tree gives. A simple lunch of fruit and bread.
Un repas frugal: a grandmother who saves string and reuses teabags.
galvanize: Galvani’s frog twitched when electricity hit it: to galvanize is to give a jolt of life.
Think of a galvanised steel bucket: coated with zinc, ready to act, hard, protected. A speech that galvanises the crowd.
gregarious: Grex (flock): the sheep that must always be with the herd. The party guest who talks to everyone.
“Greg is gregarious”: Greg always goes out with friends, never alone.
harangue: Rang: the circle of listeners around the speaker. Harangue = a long loud speech, as at a rally.
Sounds like “hurry-gang”: the coach rushing his team with a loud, long pep-talk.
iconoclast: Icon + clast (breaker): the one who smashes the holy pictures. Apple’s “Think different” rebel.
Think of a protester toppling a statue from its plinth: the iconoclast breaks what everyone else reveres.
impertinent: Not pertinent: you jump into a conversation that isn’t yours. Rude kid answering back.
In-pertinent: a cheeky remark in a meeting, out of place and disrespectful.
ingenuous: In-genuous: born in (gen = born). Naive from birth, like a child. Voltaire’s L’Ingénu.
Genuine, with no tricks: an ingenuous question from a newcomer, innocent and open.
innocuous: In + nocere (to harm): no harm done. An innocuous joke, like a water pistol.
« Anodin »: a plain grey sweater, not a danger to anyone.
intimate: As a verb: you whisper (intimus, inner) a hint, you don’t say it out loud. “He intimated he would resign.”
Not “intime”: as a verb it means to drop a hint. “She intimated that she might quit”, said by lowering her voice.
involved: Rolled up in itself (volvere, to roll): an involved plot with twists inside twists.
Un casse-tête: a long, tangled story with many subplots. Involved = complex.
laconic: Laconia = Sparta: the Spartans answered with one word. “If.” A laconic text message: “K.”
“Lacks conversation”: a laconic person says almost nothing.
maintain: Main + tenir: hold with the hand. “I maintain that I was right”: you won’t let go of your claim.
Maintain = keep up. Here, keep up an argument against opposition.
mercurial: Mercury: god of speed and the metal that rolls around. A mercurial mood: Monday joy, Tuesday gloom.
Freddie Mercury: an unpredictable, changeable performer. A mercurial temper.
parochial: Parish: the small world of one church. A parochial mind never leaves the village.
Paroissial: the local fête as the centre of the universe. Narrow outlook.
parsimonious: Pars-i-money: “parse your money”: you split each coin in two. Very stingy.
Parcimonie: Harpagon in L’Avare counting every candle. More extreme than frugal.
prevaricate: Pre + varicare (to straddle): standing with legs apart so you never choose a side. A politician who dodges the question.
Prevaricate ≈ “pre-vary-cate”: you vary your answers to avoid the truth. Tergiverser.
prodigal: The prodigal son spent everything. Prodigal = spends lavishly and carelessly.
Prodigue: the lottery winner who blows it all in a year.
profligate: Pro + fligere (strike down): you knock down your own fortune. Pure wastefulness.
“Profit-gone”: pro-fli-gate ≈ profits gone out the gate.
qualify: Add conditions: “I like it, but…”. A qualified yes is a yes with qualities (limits) attached.
In GRE contexts: to qualify a claim = to temper it. “Mostly true” instead of “true”.
restive: Rest-ive sounds restful but means the opposite: a horse that won’t stand still. A restless crowd.
Rétif: a donkey refusing to move. Restive = fidgety, hard to control.
undermine: Under + mine: dig a tunnel under the wall. Weakens slowly, from below.
A boss who undermines you in meetings, piece by piece, until your authority crumbles.
upbraid: Up + braid: you pull someone’s hair-braid up to tell them off. Scold.
Picture a teacher lifting a pupil’s braid to scold them: up + braid = a sharp telling-off.
venality: Venal = vénal: for sale, like Venus’s favours bought with coins. A bribable official.
Vend-: venality = willing to vend your integrity. Corruption.
venerate: Venus was revered: to venerate = revere deeply, as a saint or an elder.
Vénérer: candles lit in front of a statue. Deep respect.
veracious: Ver = truth (verify, verdict). Véridique: tells the truth.
Veracious ≠ voracious. Think “very true”: very + ious = very truthful.
vindicate: Vindicate = venger: you’re proved right, which feels like revenge. The data vindicated her.
“Vin-dic-ate”: the judge says “not guilty”. Cleared of blame.
wanting: Wanting = lacking something. “Found wanting”: weighed on the scale and not enough.
The adjective “wanting” is the verb’s lack: the soup is wanting salt.
